title: Shared: telemetry, the game window, screen capture, native C and her profile
tagline: What every layer may import: files, geometry, telemetry, capture, C kernels, who plays
summary: The modules outside the layer packages that any layer may import (tests/test_architecture.py's SHARED set): where files live, how the game's 1366x768 view maps to pixels, the JSON-lines telemetry every process writes and the UI reads, the game window and screen capture, the hand-written C, AVX2 and Direct3D 11 kernels that make 30-frames-a-second perception possible, garbage-collection timing, and the character profile that says who plays. They depend on no layer, so they form the base of the stack.
details_md:
**What counts as shared.** `tests/test_architecture.py` lists `capture, character, classes, directions, gcstats, native, paths, screen, telemetry, window` as SHARED and checks that every other top-level module belongs to a layer. Each layer may import these besides its allowed lower layers. Three more rules from that test shape this slice: the profiles (`character`, `classes`) import nothing of gamelab but `paths` and each other, so every layer may read them; the elevated key player must not load `native` (it would load a DLL built from the tree into an administrator process); and only `perception/frames.py` calls `capture.shared()`, because only the perception service captures the game.

**Files and geometry.** `paths` names every file; most inter-process signalling is plain files in the git-ignored `gamelab/lab/` (plans in `inbox/`, results in `outbox/`, `STOP`, `ALARM.json`, the `GPU` switch). `screen.Geometry` converts between screen px, look-frame px and map units for the window size in hand, since the game moved from a stretched 1920x1080 window to its own 1366x768 on 2026-10-23. `directions` gives left and right signs. `__init__` pins OpenBLAS to one thread (3 GB per process otherwise).

**Telemetry.** Any code calls `telemetry.emit(topic, **data)`; a process that called `record_to` gets one JSON line per record in `lab/telemetry/<time>-<command>.jsonl`, written every 0.2 s by a background thread so disk stalls never freeze a loop. 24 topics cover what the stack sees (`scene`, `tracks`, `exp`, `drops`), plans (`route`, `chain`, `sweep`, `hunt`), does (`attack`, `moved`, `trip`) and how it runs (`perf`, `gc`, `log`, `event`). The UI follows the newest file live; analysis tools read whole runs. `gcstats` adds GC counts and pauses to the service's console and a `gc` topic.

**Seeing the game.** `window` finds the game, its client rectangle, whether anything covers it, and focuses it without keys; `capture` grabs boxes of that rectangle through DXGI desktop duplication (frames handed over as shown, with their present time) or mss as a fallback.

**The C pieces.** `native.py` compiles each C source with MSVC 2022 on first use into `gamelab/build/<stem>-<hash>.dll` and loads it with ctypes (which releases Python's lock). Each piece replaces a measured hot spot. Where a Python or OpenCV fallback exists it gives that fallback's answers to the bit, except the masked match, which works out OpenCV's score exactly where OpenCV rounds in float32. Two have no fallback in the frame loop: without spawns.c the spawn watch is left out, without exact.c there is no exact finder.

| Source | Replaces | Gain measured |
|---|---|---|
| native.c | OpenCV's masked matchTemplate; per-monster re-find tasks; numpy peaks; Python flight | the masked match about 4x OpenCV's (a re-find window 0.45 vs 1.57 ms); with the one-call re-finds 30 fps in a crowd vs 14 |
| search.c | the monster search's step 1 in numpy/OpenCV | a crowded whole screen 116 -> 20 ms of CPU |
| locate.c | her plate and body cues in numpy | the body search was 7-80 ms of Python |
| camreg.c | camera registration costs in numpy | a frame 10-20 -> 0.2-0.4 ms |
| spawns.c | the spawn watch's blend sums | numpy 13.6 ms a frame (p99 132) |
| exact.c | nothing (new): an exact-pixel monster finder beside the search | 3.6 ms a frame on one thread (median, offline) |
| gpumatch.c + .hlsl | the re-finds on the GPU, same answers | off by default: slower at idle clocks |

**Who plays.** `character.active()` resolves the one character a process plays (`--character`/`GAMELAB_CHARACTER`, `lab/character.json`, config.toml, the thief) and builds her profile from `classes/thief.py` or `classes/magician.py`: attacks and their geometry, the `Shape` localization's trackers use, her files (`paths.of`), pet, policy and priors.

modules.title: Package init
modules.tagline: Pins numpy's BLAS to one thread before numpy is first imported
modules.summary: The package's only code: it sets OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS to 1 (unless already set) as gamelab is imported, before anything imports numpy. It exists because of a memory incident, not for speed.
modules.details_md:
OpenBLAS (numpy's BLAS, from `environment.yml`) commits a work buffer per thread when numpy loads: about **3 GB a Python process** with this PC's 24 hardware threads, against 18 MB with one. On 2026-10-24 a few such Python processes running at once ran the machine out of commit charge.

Nothing in gamelab needs threaded BLAS (the heavy work is OpenCV, the C pieces in `native`, or single small numpy operations), so the package sets `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1` with `os.environ.setdefault` before numpy is first imported. The conda environment's `sitecustomize.py` does the same, and the babysitter's start lines in `gamelab/README.md` set it on the command line too (`set OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1&& ... -m gamelab perceive`), so it holds even for a process that imports numpy before gamelab.

modules.title: Paths
modules.tagline: Where every file lives: config, assets, and the git-ignored lab folder
modules.summary: A table of module constants naming every file and folder gamelab uses: the repo, config.toml, the assets in git, and the working files under gamelab/lab (git-ignored). It also answers 'her own files' per character (`of`, `Files`) and per window size (`calibrated`).
modules.details_md:
`paths.py` holds no logic beyond naming. Everything a process writes for another process or for later lives under `gamelab/lab/` (`LAB`), and most inter-process signalling is plain files there:

| Constant | File | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `INBOX`, `OUTBOX` | `lab/inbox/`, `lab/outbox/` | key plans waiting for the elevated key player, and its results |
| `STOP` | `lab/STOP` | create it to stop the player |
| `GPU` | `lab/GPU` | create it to put the re-finds' matches on the GPU (`native.GPU`; `GAMELAB_GPU` wins) |
| `ALARM` | `lab/ALARM.json` | the Lie Detector was seen; nothing runs until it's cleared |
| `PLAYER_INFO` | `lab/player.json` | what the running player can do (`splice`, `pid`, `started`) |
| `TELEMETRY` | `lab/telemetry/` | one JSON-lines file per run (`telemetry`) |
| `HUNT`, `STOP_HUNT` | `lab/hunt.json`, `lab/stop_hunt.json` | the hunt running now; `gamelab stop` |
| `RECORDINGS`, `RECENT`, `ALARM_CLIPS`, `LIE_RECORDINGS` | folders | recordings: on request, the rolling recorder's saves, each alarm's clip, each Lie Detector cycle |

**Her own files.** Since the magician arrived (2026-10-27) some files belong to a character: `MINE` maps 14 lower-case names (`calibration`, `tag_template`, `tag_full`, `heading`, `heading_seed`, `heading_shots`, `shot_log`, `probe_log`, `hit_log`, `touches`, `stats`, `pet`, `grounds`, `damage`) to the module constants. `of(character)` returns a `Files` for the character (default: `character.active()`), and `Files.__getattr__` resolves a name: for the thief (folder `""`) the constant itself, exactly as before profiles existed; for another character the same file name under `lab/characters/<folder>/`, and for `heading_seed` `assets/heading_<folder>.npz`. It reads the module's globals at call time, so a test that monkeypatches a constant moves the character's file too. `Files.lab` is her own folder: `lab/` for the thief, `lab/characters/<folder>/` for another (made by whatever saves there first, normally `calibrate`, which L0 runs first: analysis.calibration).

**Per window size.** `calibrated(path, suffix)` names the calibration's files for another client size than 1920x1080: `calibration_1366x768.json` etc. (`screen.Geometry.suffix`), because her name tag and her pictures are drawn at the game's size.

modules.title: Screen geometry
modules.tagline: How the game's 1366x768 view maps onto the window and onto look frames
modules.summary: The game lays out a 1366x768 view (one game px per map unit) and stretches it to its window's client area. `Geometry` says, for a client size, how screen px, look-frame px and map units relate, and converts the px constants measured on the old 1920x1080 window into the current one. Every layer that reads pixels goes through it.
modules.details_md:
**Why it exists.** Until 2026-10-23 the game ran in a 1920x1080 client area on a 4K screen: the 1366x768 view stretched 1.40625 times with bilinear filtering, and every template, calibration and pixel constant was measured on that stretched picture. Since then the game runs at its own 1366x768, drawn pixel for pixel (the user: "run detection on the native resolution, it's both more accurate and less resource consuming"). Rather than re-measure every constant, a `Geometry` converts them.

**The model.** A `Geometry` is `client` (width, height in screen px) and `look_scale` (how much a look shrinks the client picture). From those:
- `stretch` = client height / 768: screen px per map unit (1.40625 at 1920x1080, 1 at 1366x768); `stretch_x` the same across (1920/1366 = 1.4056).
- `frame_scale` = stretch / look_scale: look-frame px per map unit (0.703 at 1920x1080 half size, 1 at 1366x768 full size); `units_per_px` its inverse.
- `px(n)` and `fpx(n)`: n screen px (or half-size frame px) of the 1920x1080 window converted to this geometry. At 1920x1080 they return n exactly, so old behaviour is unchanged.
- `to_game(p)` = (p + 0.5) / stretch - 0.5: a screen px's middle in game px, the bilinear stretch undone; `from_game` the reverse.
- `hud_top`: where monsters and drops stop being searched (the chat box and bars): 0.88 of the height at 1920x1080 as always, else game row 700 of 768 (`HUD_TOP_GAME`, measured on every 1366x768 frame of 2026-10-23 and 24; the old 0.88 would leave 25 rows above the chat box unsearched, where Tree Dungeon's platforms 31 and 32 show).
- `suffix`: empty at 1920x1080, else `_<width>x<height>` (`_1366x768`): what per-size files are told apart by (paths.calibrated).

**Look scales.** `LOOK_SCALES`: at 1920x1080 a look is half size (960x540, enough for monsters and drops at a quarter of the pixels); at 1366x768 full size (about twice 960x540's pixels at 1.42 times the detail). Any other size: 2.

**Where it travels.** A geometry is made from the frame actually in hand (`of_frame`), and rides along with what is read from it (`perception.eyes.Observation.geo`, `Scene`, `WorldState.geo`), so nothing assumes a size. `STRETCHED`'s numbers (`GAME_SIZE`, `SCREEN_SCALE`, `SCALE`, `UNITS_PER_HALF_PX`) are kept only for the simulator, which draws its world at 1920x1080, and for old screenshots; `tests/test_geometry.py` checks that nothing reading the game uses them or uses a `*_PX` constant unconverted.

modules.title: Directions
modules.tagline: Left and right as strings, and their sign along map x
modules.summary: Three helpers over maplehelper.engine's LEFT and RIGHT ('left', 'right', also the arrow keys' names): the sign of a direction along map x, the direction of a step, and the opposite direction.
modules.details_md: Map x grows to the right, so `sign(RIGHT)` is +1 and `sign(LEFT)` is -1. `toward(dx)` names the direction of a step along x (RIGHT for a positive dx, LEFT otherwise, including 0), and `opposite` flips one. Directions are plain strings everywhere in gamelab (facings in telemetry, arrow keys in key plans), which is why the constants come from `maplehelper.engine` rather than an enum: they double as key names. Used by perception (heading), motion (route, flow), attack (stance), control (actions, mover, navigator), behavior, the simulator and the UI renderer. Keeping these three one-liners in one shared module means every layer agrees on the convention (x grows to the right, a step of 0 counts as LEFT) without importing another layer.

modules.title: Telemetry
modules.tagline: Every process's record of what it saw and did, as JSON lines the UI follows
modules.summary: Producers anywhere call `emit(topic, **data)`; once a process installs a recorder (`record_to`), each record becomes one JSON line `{"t", "topic", ...}` appended by a background writer thread to `lab/telemetry/<time>-<name>.jsonl`. The mini-map window and web page follow the newest file live (`newest`, `Follower`); analysis tools read whole files (`read`). Files roll into parts and the folder is pruned to 2 GB.
modules.details_md:
**Producing.** `emit` is a no-op until a recorder is installed, so tests and library use pay nothing (`recording()` lets callers skip building unseen records; `captured()` collects them in a list for tests). `t` is wall-clock time to the ms (the simulator's clock in a sim run), so a replay keeps the original pace. Telemetry never stops a run: a record that can't be serialised or written stops recording with one warning.

**Writing off the loops.** A `Recorder` makes the line where it's emitted (compact `json.dumps`, numpy values made plain) and queues it; its `telemetry-writer` thread writes and flushes the batch every `FLUSH_S` = 0.2 s. Since 2026-10-26 a disk stall can't freeze the frame loop or a hunt (on 2026-10-25/26 both stood still 0.5-2 s now and then, plausibly synchronous SSD writes). Past `QUEUE_LINES` = 50,000 waiting (about 2 hours of the service) records are dropped and counted. `console_in_background()` does the same for the perception service's stdout/stderr.

**Parts and retention.** Past `MAX_BYTES` = 64 MiB a run continues in `...-<name>-part2.jsonl`, named at least a second after the previous part and headed by the run's `session` record with `continues` and `part`. When a run or part starts, `prune` deletes the oldest files until the rest fit `KEEP_BYTES` = 2 GiB (`watch` writes about 400 MB a day), never the part being written; none goes for age alone, since old telemetry is evidence later fits use.

**Following.** `newest()` finds the file written last. On NTFS `os.scandir`'s time is the directory's copy, updated only when a file is opened or closed, so files it says changed within `RECENT_S` (7 days) are asked `os.stat`. Names aren't compared: they're local time and sort wrong when clocks go back. `Follower.poll()` reads from its last offset, holding back a half-written line.

**The topics** (map units; producers build the records, `ui.state` folds them):

| Topic | Main fields | Written by |
|---|---|---|
| `session` | map, command, mode; continues, part; physics | each run and part |
| `motion` | old/new walk and climb, speed, why | behavior.hunter (from 2026-11-02) |
| `scene` | her {x, y, platform, facing...}, hp, mp, monsters, loot, view, players | every look; `watch` 10/s |
| `tracks` | tracks {id, kind, state, x, y, vx, bar, cause, gain...} | `watch`, perception service, 2/s |
| `exp` | exp, level, gain, kinds, per_minute | each EXP gain |
| `drops` | pending piles, inventory_full | every look |
| `glance` | x, y, hp | navigator, during a chain |
| `route` | dst, moves, from, keep_off, ways, chose | navigator, each plan |
| `chain` | why, text, legs | navigator, each key plan |

| `monsters` | platform, x, vx, heading, reach | navigator |
| `trip` | dst, result, on, x, walk | navigator, each trip's end |
| `attack` | key, why, kind, hp, mp, track, side | behavior.attacks, each throw |
| `no_cast` | why, kind, track, mp, cost | behavior.attacks |
| `sweep` | dest, candidates, order, budget | behavior.hunt |

modules.title: GC timing
modules.tagline: Python's garbage collections counted and timed, said live
modules.summary: Hooks `gc.callbacks` to count each generation's collections and time their pauses, per reader. The perception service ends its 10 s console line with them and every recording process writes a `gc` telemetry record once a minute, so a lag can be told from a collection live. `freeze` moves everything into the permanent generation when a run is made.
modules.details_md:
**Why.** On 2026-10-26 the user asked whether the hunts' lags were Python's GC and proposed a full port. Measured first: the service's frame loop replayed made 207 collections in 1,622 s (0.0037% of the time, the longest 4.2 ms), a simulated hunt 0.016-0.018%, no full collection in 40 minutes. The lag was the frame loop running out of CPU (fixed by the C pieces, `native`). This module keeps that question answerable live and would show a growing collection (a run's objects piling up).

**How.** `GcStats.callback` is appended to `gc.callbacks` once (`install`). On `start` it stamps `perf_counter`; on `stop` it adds the pause to the totals and to every reader's open window (`_Window`: counts per generation, total pause, longest, since). It takes **no lock**: a collection can start in any thread at any allocation, including inside `take`, and a callback waiting for a lock its own thread holds would hang the process (the 2026-10-26 review hung it so with the collector's threshold at 1 and 50). Instead it copies the windows with `list(dict.values())` and mutates each in place. `take(reader)` swaps in a fresh window (made before taking the lock, which only guards readers from each other) and returns `{collections, pause_ms, longest_ms, seconds, frozen}`. `line()` words it for a console: "GC 4 (gen 0, 1, 2: 3, 1, 0), 0.6 ms, the longest 0.3".

**Freeze.** `freeze()` unfreezes, collects, then `gc.freeze()`s every object: the perception service does it as each run is made, so no later collection walks the map's templates, models and modules (47,600-48,200 objects in 14-31 ms on the replay; after it 0.05-0.7 collections a second, the longest 0.99 ms, none of the oldest generation).

**Reporting.** `report_every(emit, seconds=60, reader='telemetry', when=...)` starts one daemon thread per process (`gc-report`) that emits a `gc` record every minute while `when()` is true (`telemetry.to_file`: never into a test's captured records). `__main__` calls it for every command that records telemetry and for `perceive`.

modules.title: The game window
modules.tagline: Find the game window, its client area, what covers it; focus it; move the pointer
modules.summary: Win32 calls through ctypes: the game window's handle and client rectangle (the capture area), whether it is minimized, full screen, on screen or covered by another program's window, resizing its client to an allowed size, bringing it to the front without sending keys, and moving the mouse along a human-like trail. The elevated key player imports it, so it loads only the standard library and maplehelper's input helpers.
modules.details_md:
**Where the game is.** `find_game(title)` is `FindWindowW`; `client_rect` returns the client area in screen px as an mss-style dict `{left, top, width, height}`: the box every capture takes. `window_rect` is the outer box (on 2026-10-25 23:40 the game drew its picture at that box's corner, which `perception.framecheck` checks for). `full_screen` compares the client area with its monitor's rectangle; `on_screen` checks each corner is on some monitor (after Chrome Remote Desktop resizes the desktop a window can hang off it, where `WindowFromPoint` finds nothing and `shows` would call it covered).

**Is anything over it?** Captures see whatever is on top, so frames of a covered game must not be used or recorded. `shows(hwnd, area)` asks `WindowFromPoint` at the middle and four inset corners (or a grid). That misses windows between the points and click-through layered overlays, so `over` / `overs` walk the z-order upward from the game (`GetWindow(GW_HWNDPREV)`, at most `OVER_MAX` = 2000 steps) and report any visible, non-minimized, non-cloaked (`DWMWA_CLOAKED`) window of another process whose drawn box (`DWMWA_EXTENDED_FRAME_BOUNDS`) meets the client area: 0.1 ms with 39 windows above the game (2026-10-24). Windows of processes in `GAME_FAMILY` (`nexon_client.exe`) count as the game's own: on 2026-10-29 the Nexon launcher's invisible, topmost, click-through overlay made every frame of a night "covered". `describe` names a window by class and box, never its title (which can say what's in it). `overs` lists every covering window with its box, and `client_boxes` cuts those boxes to the client area, which the rolling recording notes with a frame instead of dropping it. `pointer_on(hwnd)` says whether the window under the mouse pointer is the game's (a click there would be its).

**Focus.** `bring_to_front(title, wait)` restores a minimized game, attaches to the foreground window's input thread (Windows lets only the foreground's owner hand focus away), calls `BringWindowToTop` + `SetForegroundWindow`, then polls every `FRONT_POLL_S` = 50 ms. `SetForegroundWindow` can fail silently under the foreground lock (2026-10-21 01:01:30: the player refused a plan, "game not in front (foreground: 'Claude')"), so with `SWITCH_FALLBACK` it calls `SwitchToThisWindow` once half the wait has passed. It sends no keys and clicks nothing.

**Size.** `resize_client` sets the client to one of `CLIENT_SIZES` (1366x768 or 1920x1080) with `AdjustWindowRectEx` + `SetWindowPos`, keeping the top-left corner. The game runs as administrator, so only the elevated player can ("access denied" otherwise, tried 2026-10-23).

**Pointer.** `move_cursor(x, y, wait, played)` follows `maplehelper.mouse_trail.generate_trail` with one whole-pixel `send_mouse_move` per sample, sleeping until each is due, or using the player's plan-aware `wait(due)` which can return a stop or a splice; a final `SetCursorPos` removes `SendInput`'s sub-pixel rounding. `played` collects `[time, x, y]` for the review overlay of the Lie Detector's cursor (2026-11-03). `last_input_age` (GetLastInputInfo) tells behavior.guard how long the session has been idle.

modules.title: Screen capture
modules.tagline: Boxes of the screen as BGRA arrays, via DXGI desktop duplication or mss
modules.summary: A `Grabber` takes `Shot`s of the screen: with DXGI desktop duplication (default) it holds the monitor's newest frame on the graphics card with the time it was shown, and copies boxes off the card on request; when that fails it falls back to mss (GDI) for 10 s. One shared grabber per process (`shared`), used only by perception/frames.py, i.e. the perception service; the rolling recorder makes its own mss-only `Grabber("mss")` so it holds no duplication. Pure ctypes COM calls, no extra packages.
modules.details_md:
**Why DXGI.** mss copies with GDI, which waits for the compositor's next frame: 16.7 ms a grab whatever the box, 17-46 ms after a pause, so a glance of two boxes took 33 ms. Desktop duplication is handed each frame as the monitor shows it, with its present time in QueryPerformanceCounter ticks (the clock `time.monotonic` reads; `qpc_offset` measures the offset rather than assuming 0). Measured with `bench-capture` (on the desktop, the game not running): a look's capture 12.4 ms vs 24.5 with mss, a glance 1.0 ms vs 33.7, the pixels mss's exactly.

**Freshness.** A look must see the result of the keys sent before it, so `Grabber.shot(area, after=t)` asks for a frame shown at or after `t`. `Duplicator.advance` loops on `AcquireNextFrame`, waiting at most `FRESH_WAIT_S` = 20 ms for one; if none comes, nothing on screen changed and the held frame is the screen as it is. (15 ms was shorter than a game frame: 6-18% of looks got a frame shown 1-3 ms before they began.) Waits end on Windows' 15.6 ms timer ticks, so a static screen costs 31 ms, but the game's screen always moves. Frames with no present time (the black first frame after duplicating, or pointer-only updates) don't count; the first real frame is waited for up to `FIRST_FRAME_S` = 0.25 s.

**On the card.** `Dxgi.acquire` copies each new frame into a texture of its own (`_last`) and releases DXGI's at once. `Dxgi.read(boxes)` copies each box into a staging texture (`CopySubresourceRegion`), maps it and hands numpy views to `convert` (or copies): converting straight from the mapped copy took 2.0 ms for a whole RGB frame instead of 3.8. With `[capture] fence = true` (off by default, not tried live, since 2026-10-27) the copy is waited for on an `ID3D11Fence` event for up to `COPY_WAIT_MS` = 100 ms before `Map`, whose own wait spins an NVIDIA driver thread (process CPU 4.96-5.17 ms a frame vs 1.04-1.07 on the event, the frame 0.15-0.2 ms later).

**Failure handling.** `DXGI_ERROR_ACCESS_LOST` (a UAC prompt, a mode change, a full-screen switch) re-duplicates once (180-240 ms). Anything else raises `CaptureError`; `Grabber.failed` closes the duplication and uses mss for `RETRY_S` = 10 s. An area spanning monitors, a rotated monitor, or a box off the monitor also goes to mss. `reopen` and `fall_back` let perception.framecheck force a fresh duplication or mss when a frame doesn't line up with the window.

**One per process.** Only one duplication of a monitor can be open in a process, so `shared()` hands out one Grabber; a `DxgiShot` is only valid until the grabber's next shot (`seq`). Windows also limits duplications across processes (a third failed with 0x887A0022), which is why `tests/test_architecture.py` allows `capture.shared()` only in `perception/frames.py`: the perception service is the one process that captures the game. The elevated key player keeps mss.

modules.title: Native loader
modules.tagline: Builds gamelab's C sources into DLLs on first use and wraps them for Python
modules.summary: The Python side of gamelab's C pieces: it compiles each .c source with MSVC 2022 into a DLL named for its source's hash, loads it with ctypes, declares every function's signature, and wraps the calls (masked template match, step-1 peaks, a frame's re-finds in one call, her flight, the GPU switch). Every caller still works when a DLL is missing: numpy/OpenCV give the same answers, slower, except that without spawns.c the frame step leaves the spawn watch out and without exact.c there is no exact finder.
modules.details_md:
**The DLLs.**

| Source | Loader | What it speeds up | Needs AVX2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| native.c (+ gpumatch.c, gpumatch.hlsl) | `lib()` | masked colour match, re-finds in one call, step-1 peaks, her flight | masked match only |
| search.c | `search_lib()` | the monster search's step 1 | yes (`sr_ready`) |
| locate.c | `locate_lib()` | her name plate and body cues | yes (`lc_ready`) |
| spawns.c | `spawns_lib()` | the spawn watch's blend sums | yes (`sp_ready`) |
| exact.c | `exact_lib()` | the exact-pixel monster finder | no (plain C) |
| camreg.c | `localization/camreg.py` via `native.build` | camera registration costs | runtime choice |

**Building.** `build(source)` returns `gamelab/build/<stem>-<sha1[:12]>.dll`, the hash over the source (plus gpumatch.c/.hlsl for native.c) and the flags, building it if absent: `cmd /d /s /c` runs `vcvars64.bat` from the VS 2022 Build Tools then `cl /nologo /O2 /fp:precise /MT /LD` in a temp dir, with gpumatch.hlsl written as a C string header (`gpumatch_hlsl.h`, compiled at run time by d3dcompiler_47). `/fp:precise` keeps IEEE arithmetic in source order (no fused multiply-adds) so answers match Python's to the bit; `/MT` links the C runtime in. An edited source gets a new DLL, a DLL another process has loaded is never overwritten, and older builds of the same stem are deleted when possible. `python -m gamelab.native` builds them all and says where.

**Loading.** Each `*_lib()` builds and loads once a process under `_lock` (the search's threads ask at once), sets `restype`/`argtypes` from its SIGNATURES table, asks the CPU check where there is one, and on any failure records why (`why`, `search_why`, ...) and returns None for good. `USE = False` turns them all off. ctypes releases Python's lock during each call, which is half the point: numpy and the Python around OpenCV held it.

**The wrappers.** `prepare_masked` makes a template + mask ready once (`Masked`: sums, mask runs, rows as int16, and an NTT transform when it fits a 128x128 plane); only with AVX2, since plain C was 3.4-3.7x slower than OpenCV. `masked_match` / `best_matches` return OpenCV's TM_CCOEFF_NORMED-with-mask scores worked out exactly. `peaks` is step 1's cover test + 8-neighbour peak pick. `Refinds` wraps native.c's `rf_*` contract: a detector's prepared pictures, a thread pool made once, per-track memos; `start`/`next`/`end` let the caller do each job's Python while others are matched. `Map`, `Walls`, `shoe_of` and `fly` lay out a map's platforms for her flight in C (motion.physics). `shrink_area` is cv2.resize's INTER_AREA through search.c's `sr_shrink` (the same bytes; None where the C declines), and `SrUnit`, `SrShape`, `SrGroup` are the ctypes mirrors of search.c's structs that perception.mobs fills.

**The GPU switch.** `gpu_mode()` reads `GAMELAB_GPU` (`0`, `1`, `ahead`) or the file `lab/GPU` (empty: `start`; the text `ahead`: `ahead`), the file because a process started through WMI inherits no environment. `GPU` and `AHEAD` are read at import and passed to the DLL (`gm_on`, `gm_ahead`) when it loads. Off by default: on this machine's RTX 3080 it doesn't pay. `state()`, `search_state()` and `gpu_line()` are what the perception service prints so a DLL that failed to build shows as more than "fewer frames a second".

modules.title: native.c: masked match, re-finds, flight
modules.tagline: Exact masked template matching, a frame's re-finds in one threaded call, her flight
modules.summary: The main C DLL. It computes OpenCV's masked TM_CCOEFF_NORMED exactly in integers (AVX2 place by place, or all places at once by number-theoretic transform), runs all of a frame's monster re-finds in one call on its own thread pool with per-track memos (and the GPU backend from gpumatch.c behind the same contract), picks step 1's silhouette peaks, and steps her flight 5 ms at a time exactly as the Python physics does.
modules.details_md:
**The masked match** (`mm_*`, for `perception/match.py`). With n the mask's pixels, the template's per-channel sums ST_c and STT_c (made once by `mm_prepare`), and at each place STI (template x image dot product), S1_c and S2 (the image's sums under the mask):

```
N = n STI - sum_c ST_c S1_c    A = sum_c (n STT_c - ST_c^2)    B = n S2 - sum_c S1_c^2   (exact int64)
score = N / sqrt(A B)  (double, then float32); -1 where A B is 0 (a flat window)
```

OpenCV sums in float32 through FFTs, so its scores differ in the last bits (within 9.5e-7 colour, 2.5e-5 brightness on a crowd's 1,293 matches; the 0.55/0.6/0.9 threshold decisions identical). The dot products go one of two exact ways: `dots_avx2` does 16 int16 products per madd, 8 places at once sharing each template load, only over the 16-wide chunks the mask covers (at the madd's own pace: 0.42 ns per madd on the Ryzen 9 5900X); or, when places x chunks reach `NTT_LEAST` = 300,000 (a re-find's ~98x102 window around a ~52x56 picture: 912,000), every place at once as a correlation by number-theoretic transform on 128x128 planes modulo 998,244,353 (Montgomery arithmetic, AVX2 lanes, no reordering pass). Templates whose dot products could reach the prime get no transform. The mask's sums come from per-channel prefix sums, a run of mask pixels at a time, 24 places in AVX2 registers. Scratch memory is thread-local and kept between calls. AVX2 is detected at run time (`has_avx2`, `mm_simd`); the build has no /arch flag so the other pieces stay bit-exact.

Speed: a re-find window 0.45 ms vs OpenCV's 1.57; a step-2 check 0.05 vs 0.58; a drop's strip 0.28 vs 0.68. With the transform, against the same C place by place, a re-find call took 0.31 ms vs 0.61 (median) and a frame's re-finds 6.2-6.5 ms vs 17.3-17.6 (mean).

**A frame's re-finds in one call** (`rf_*`, for `MobDetector.refind_all`). The contract comment above `RfJob` is binding for any backend: each job (a followed monster) has an id (its memo), a near and a full window, and two picture lists (the last match; the animation's likely next frames). In a window the first pictures are tried, one becoming best if it scores at least `thr` and above the best so far as rounded to 3 decimals (Python's `round`, `rf_round3`); then the next pictures until one scores `good`. The near window answers if its best is over `good` and at least `ngood`; else the full window. A memo answers a window whose position, pictures and pixels are byte-identical to last time. Jobs are taken largest first by the pool's threads and by the caller in `rf_next`; `rf_start` / `rf_next` / `rf_end` let Python do each job's own part (kind check, fallback) as answers arrive.

**Step 1 peaks** (`silhouette_peaks`): the cover test from an integral image and the 3x3 peak rule, which in numpy held the GIL (18 ms of a band search's 34). **Her flight** (`fly`): body.air_step's drag, gravity and steering, walls and landing tests in IEEE double in Python's order (min/max written out so even a zero's sign matches), up to `MAX_PLATFORMS` = 4096; the planner flies some 25,000 flights to build a map's moves, about 1 ms each in Python.

modules.title: search.c: the monster search's step 1
modules.tagline: A band's colour tests, silhouette scores and peaks in a few calls
modules.summary: Step 1 of the whole-screen monster search (perception/mobs.py) in C with AVX2: shrink the band like OpenCV's INTER_AREA, run every kind's colour test, score each silhouette only where the cover test keeps a window and its score can reach the threshold, pick the peaks and the places step 2 checks. A crowd's whole screen fell from 116 ms of CPU to 20.
modules.details_md:
**Why.** In numpy/OpenCV step 1 took 116 ms of CPU per crowded screen on one thread, 82 of it OpenCV's `matchTemplate` over 4.07 M windows of which the cover test then kept only 3.6% (the profile of 2026-10-27). On its thread in the service a whole screen took 55-69 ms (median); now 14-17, about 0.4 of a core less in a crowd, and an ask for it is answered in 26-28 ms instead of 61-84.

**The calls** (Python's lock released for each):
- `sr_shrink`: OpenCV 5.0.0's INTER_AREA resize to step 1's scale, its float32 arithmetic in its order (the same bytes as cv2.resize; tests compare).
- `sr_colours` / `sr_step1`: every kind's colour test 16 pixels at a time (four hand-made tests: slime, pig, snail, orange mushroom; or the learned gates' table, up to 15 kinds as bits), I4 = count of the kind's pixels in each 2x2 cell (the coarse picture is I4 / 4 exactly), integral images, then each silhouette scored **exactly**: T_int = T x 2^shift, N = n S_I4T - S_I4 S_T, A = n S_TT - S_T^2, B = n S_I4I4 - S_I4^2, score = N / sqrt(A B) rounded once to float32. A window is skipped only where an upper bound of its score (from its colour by rows, then columns, then exact products a few rows at a time, the rows of most template mass first) plus the bound of OpenCV's float32 noise (nk n sqrt(S_I4I4 S_TT)/sqrt(A B) + n0: `mobs.NOISE_K`, `NOISE_ABS`) falls under the threshold, so it can't be a peak in either and stops no neighbour from being one. Peaks follow native.c's rule; a shape is flagged where OpenCV's noise could change master's peaks (ties, neighbours within bounds, a score near the threshold), and Python then works it out as master does.
- `sr_places`: master's sort of (score, cx, cy, i) tuples and its place picking.

Shapes of one size are grouped (`SrGroup`, up to `GL` = 16, one int16 lane each) so their bound tables are checked side by side. A silhouette over 64 x 256 cells, sums past 2^52, or a kind with a colour test the C doesn't know leaves its detector to numpy/OpenCV.

modules.title: locate.c: her plate and body cues
modules.tagline: Exact colour counts of her name plate and pixel-by-pixel pose agreement
modules.summary: The inner loops of the two cues that place her on screen when her gray name-tag match is unsure: her name plate's exact colours counted at every place of a window (perception/plate.py), and her body's poses checked pixel by pixel (perception/poses.py). Integer counts only, so the numpy fallback gives the same answers.
modules.details_md:
Ported from the localization prototype of 2026-10-29, whose body search took 7-80 ms of Python and had to run on the 15-a-second search thread (the user: "port the localization to C ... do that quickly as I can really benefit from it").

**Her plate** (`lc_plate`): the plate item is drawn bit-exact, so every pixel gets a palette index (the plate's own colours via a perfect multiplicative hash of their 24-bit codes; `NONE` = 255 for anything else; rows from the HUD down are none). At each place the count of the plate's stable pixels (1,395 of its 114x33 box, 40 colours) whose exact colour the frame has is summed 32 places a step, a byte compare per plate pixel. Places in the minimap are zeroed, the best `topk` kept with their neighbourhoods suppressed (cv2.minMaxLoc's order), and at each (the first refined +-1 px) the evidence: plate pixels matched, her letters white, white where her name has none, letters in column bins all shown (`clean`). `lc_plate_counts` gives the counts alone.

**Her body** (`lc_pack` + `lc_agree`): a box of the frame packed one int32 per pixel (thread-local), then for each candidate pose (its pixels at her feet's column and row) and each offset within +-R, the share of its pixels within tolerance on every channel, as drawn or as the post-touch blink darkens her (the better of the two). modules.tagline: Integer sums of the blend fit of monsters fading in at spawn points
modules.summary: The spawn watch (perception/spawns.py) fits each newborn monster's opacity as it fades in over the map's art. **The model** (spawns.py's top): a newborn of opacity a over the art B is drawn F = B + a (A/255)(S - B), A the game's alpha of each of its picture's pixels and S its colour. With D = F - B and G = A (S - B) for each channel of each sampled pixel, the sums D.G, G.G, D.D and the pixel count n give a = 255 D.G / G.G, the share of D.D explained (D.G)^2 / (G.G D.D), and the residual. |D| <= 255 and |G| <= 65,025, so D.G and D.D per pixel fit int32 but G.G doesn't: the sums go to int64, summed in int32 for `BLOCK` = 32 pixels first.

- `sp_empty`: how many of a window's pixels have a largest channel difference from the art over `levels` (the empty test).
- `sp_sums`: each hypothesis's sums. Hypotheses come in runs of up to 8 one column apart (the newborn's feet a unit apart along a flat stretch of platform), so after copying the window and its art into planes of their own, a run's 8 hypotheses are 8 lanes of one load per pixel and channel. A run of 1 goes one at a time.

modules.title: exact.c: the exact-pixel finder
modules.tagline: Monsters found by anchor-pair votes and exact pixel counts
modules.summary: The game draws a sprite's opaque pixels unchanged, so at the game's own 1366x768 any visible part of a monster is its picture's pixels exactly. Anchor pairs vote for (picture, offset) places; places with enough votes have their pixels compared; each frame pixel is credited to one find. Plain C, no intrinsics; used by perception/exact.py beside the masked search.
modules.details_md:
**Anchors** are pairs of side-by-side pixels of a picture, chosen by the caller (rare in the picture, their first colour sparse on the map). `ex_open` copies the pictures' masked pixels and builds a hash table of anchor keys (the six bytes of a pixel pair) plus a 15-bit colour lookup table saying whether a colour starts any anchor: most frame pixels stop there.

**`ex_find`**, per frame box: for each pixel whose colour starts an anchor, the pair's key is looked up; each matching anchor votes for (picture, ox, oy) in a generation-stamped open-addressing table (`VOTE_BITS` = 18: 262,144 entries; ids pack 10 bits of picture and 11 bits each of x and y + `OFF`). A place reaching `min_votes` (perception.exact's `MIN_VOTES` = 6) becomes a candidate; each candidate's pixels are compared exactly (`exact_at`), those with `min_exact` (`MIN_EXACT` = 200) kept, sorted most exact first, then each frame pixel is explained by one find only: going down that list, a find's `fresh` count is its exact pixels no better find already explained, and a find with fewer than `min_exact` fresh pixels is dropped, so a picture and its neighbouring animation frame (sharing most pixels) don't both count. A kept find marks its exact pixels explained; the map is cleared after the call only where it was written. Once three quarters of the vote table is in use, new places get no more entries (a frame that full of matching pairs isn't the game's).

**Measured** (2026-11-04, README "The exact finder"): 3.60 ms median, p99 7.2, on one thread on the 22:49 clip (66 pictures, 17,052 anchors). It sees monsters under her body, her pet, effects and the HUD that the masked search misses (near-her detection 38% -> 100% under 25 units). It finds nothing on a fade-in, a shade or JPEG, by design, and runs only at the game's own size.

modules.title: gpumatch.c: the re-finds on the GPU (host)
modules.tagline: A Direct3D 11 backend behind rf_* giving the CPU's answers to the bit
modules.summary: Included by native.c: a GPU backend for a frame's re-find matches. The GPU computes each place's exact integer sums and an approximate score; the CPU rescans only the places within 2 x 2^-14 of the best approximate score exactly, so every answer is the CPU's. Off by default (native.GPU) because on this PC it doesn't pay.
modules.details_md:
**What a GPU can give exactly.** Direct3D 11's shader model 5 has no 64-bit integers and no double square root, so the GPU computes per place STI, S1_c and S2 as uint32 (exact for pictures up to 128x128) and an approximate score s~ in float32, within `GM_EPS` = 2^-14 of the float32 score. Of each window's places only those within 2 GM_EPS of the highest s~ come back, at most `GM_CAND` = 32, with their sums; `gm_answer` scores them as native.c's `score_at` and takes the first highest row by row. More candidates, a picture past 128 px or flat, or any failure: that match is the CPU's (`rf_best`).

**Per call** (`gm_rf_send` at rf_start): every job's full window with every picture of its lists that fits (the near window as a sub-rectangle), windows the memo will answer left out, bytes copied into one upload buffer, three dispatches (prep, match, choose) and the candidates' copy in one submission. `rf_next` waits on the fence's event (no spinning) at most `GM_WAIT_US` = 6 ms; past that the call goes to the CPU's threads at once, and so do the next calls for `GM_REST_US` = 1 s and until the GPU has caught up. A removed device (driver reset) turns it off for the context's life.

**Never stalls a frame.** The device is made on a thread of its own (0.7 s to on, the three shaders compiled at run time by d3dcompiler_47); rf_close never waits for it. Only a hardware adapter (never WARP). d3d11, dxgi and d3dcompiler_47 are loaded at run time, so a machine without them just has no GPU path; built without the SDK headers (or `GM_NO_D3D`) the backend is only off (why 6). Buffers are made once (about 35 MB of video memory).

**Twice as fast** (later on 2026-10-27): window rows in 4 planes for coalesced loads, packed pixels, the device at the lowest GPU thread priority (`GM_PRIORITY` = -7, so the game's frames are drawn first), and `rf_ahead`: at a frame's start each followed monster's full window where the previous frame's camera puts it (2 px wider each side, 6 taller) is sent from a thread-pool callback, only each place's key coming back; rf_start never waits for it (`GM_AHEAD_WAIT_US` = 0) and each pair whose window lies inside one sent is answered from it once in.

**Why off.** The RTX 3080 idles at P8 (210 MHz) between the frame loop's calls: a crowd's frame took 5-5.3 ms there against 2.1-2.2 on the C's 4 threads, and freeing 0.15-0.25 cores made nothing measurably smoother.

modules.title: gpumatch.hlsl: the compute shaders
modules.tagline: Three cs_5_0 passes: prep, match, choose
modules.summary: The GPU side of the re-find matches: per place of a window and a picture, exact uint32 sums (STI, S1_c, S2) and an approximate float32 score; then each region's candidates near its highest score. Compiled at run time from a C string native.py embeds in the DLL.
modules.details_md:
**Exactness.** STI is summed in float32 partial sums of at most `CHUNK` = 64 pixels of a mask run: each product is an integer at most 255^2, a partial sum at most 64 x 3 x 255^2 = 12,484,800 < 2^24, so every float32 step is an exact integer, each then added into a uint. S1_c and S2 come from each window row's prefix sums, a mask run at a time. N and B are built in 64-bit integers made of two uints; s~ = N / sqrt(A B) in float32 (-1 where B is 0), within 2^-14 of the float32 score (at most 1.8e-7 measured over 42.7 M places).

**The passes** (one dispatch each, one submission a frame):
- `prep` (128 threads a group): each window's rows as packed pixels (R | G << 8 | B << 16) and uint4 prefix sums, laid out in `RUN` = 4 planes (column c at plane c % 4) so a warp's loads are side by side; tasks' records cleared.
- `match` (`GROUP` = 64 threads, RUN = 4 places side by side a thread): the sums, s~, and the highest s~ of the task and of its near sub-rectangle via `InterlockedMax` on an orderable key (`key_of`). Reads prep's output through read-only views (cached). A frame sent ahead writes only each place's key.
- `choose`: each place within `band` (2 GM_EPS) of its region's highest goes to that region's candidates (at most `kcand`).

At the RTX 3080's idle clocks (P8, 210 MHz) a crowd's call took 5.15 ms of GPU time as first built and 2.37 after the plane layout and packing (match 2.08, prep 0.21); clocked up 0.34.

modules.title: Her profile
modules.tagline: Who plays in this process, and the data the stack takes of her
modules.summary: Resolves the one character a process plays (`active`) and defines her profile as frozen dataclasses: stats, keys, attacks with their geometry, what localization takes of her attacks (`Shape`), what perception reads of her, pet, policy and planner priors. Data only: it imports nothing of gamelab but paths, so every layer may read it.
modules.details_md:
**Why.** Until 2026-10-27 gamelab hunted with one character, the thief (BugBaby: Lucky Seven and a claw's throwing stars). Then the user: "I have another character magician who will use magic claw to grind on this map ... I will switch back and forth ... so the code needs to be generalized". Magic Claw is another kind of attack (the client's stepped search for an aimed spell, from 50 ahead to 300, nothing stopping it, no flight, from the ground only), with other stats, keys, ammunition (MP) and files.

**Who plays.** `active_id` takes the first that names one: `GAMELAB_CHARACTER` (set by `--character` before any command loads `motion.physics`, which works her walk and jumps out once at import; child processes inherit it), then `lab/character.json` (`gamelab character use <id>`), then config.toml's `[characters] default`, then the thief. Under `GAMELAB_FIXED_STATS` (tests, golden traces, the harness) only the env var counts and stats are the class's fixed copy, config.toml unread. `active()` resolves once and caches, so her physics, her files (`paths.of`) and what lets a command run are one character's. Commands that act in the game play another character only when the env var names her, until her bottom bar is read.

**The profile.** `load(which)` takes her class module (`classes.thief` or `classes.magician`, by the `[characters.<id>]` table's class or the id), its `profile(id)`; for the thief, config.toml's flat `[character]` stats and Lucky Seven's level (`leveled`); for others, the table's stats over the class's fixed ones; then `configured(c, table)`. The main types:
- `AttackSpec`: key, hits, damage lo/hi, MP, ammo, the timings (lock, release, damage, lands), projectile speed, cycle, miss share, `air`, and a `Geometry` (`star_search`, `search` or `melee`).
- `Search`: the client's forward search: bands `step` = 20 wide from `start` to `range`, band k's window `row` -/+ (start + step k) // `spread` around 28 over her feet; the first band any body overlaps picks (`band`).
- `Shape`: what localization's trackers take of her attacks: nearest and farthest a picked monster's middle can be (signed), up/down, the time windows, `order` ('line' or 'band'), the look band, and `kill` (`KillCredit`: her kill bound by the client's search, the magician's).
- `Perception`: her files folder, bottom bar job and name, heading box, attack score/margin, hit effect size.
- `Policy`, `Pet`, `Buff`, `Priors`, and `safety_hits` (the safety stop's reserve of the map's largest touches). Some of these are read from the profile itself (behavior.hunter takes `safety_hits`, `pet.hp_warning` and `policy`; control.navigator and attack.magic take `policy.close_quarters`), others only describe constants that live elsewhere (the thief's).

`describe` prints a profile for `gamelab character`; `stats_from` says where a stat came from (the hunter's note when her stat window disagrees).

flows.title: How a telemetry record reaches the mini-map
flows.summary: A command starts recording, any layer emits records, a background thread writes them in batches, and the UI follows the newest file.
flows.trigger: A command that records telemetry starts (__main__ calls telemetry.record_to(command) and gcstats.report_every).

steps.text: Prunes lab/telemetry/ to the newest 2 GiB, then installs a Recorder on <YYYYmmdd-HHMMSS>-<name>.jsonl with its telemetry-writer thread.
A layer calls emit('scene', her=..., monsters=...): {t, topic, **data} goes to the sink; nothing happens without a recorder.
The record is serialised compactly (numpy values made plain) and queued; past 50,000 waiting it's dropped and counted.
Every 0.2 s the writer thread writes the batch under the file lock and flushes; past 64 MiB _next_part opens part N headed by the session record.
The mini-map / web server finds the newest run (telemetry.newest, os.stat for recent files) and reads what was appended (telemetry.Follower.poll), holding back a half-written line.
Each record is folded into the UI's State (latest record per topic, her trail, the log) and drawn.

flows.title: How a look's pixels come off the screen
flows.summary: The perception service asks the shared Grabber for a frame shown after a moment; DXGI hands frames over on the GPU, boxes are copied off the card; failures fall back to mss.
flows.trigger: The perception service's frame loop needs the next frame (ScreenFrames.next(after)).

steps.text: Takes the game's client rectangle (window.client_rect) as the Area and asks the process's grabber (capture.shared) for a shot shown after `after`.
Under the grabber's lock: DXGI unless a failure put it on mss for RETRY_S; _duplicator opens (or moves) the duplication of the monitor holding the area's centre, None if it spans monitors.

Loops AcquireNextFrame: frames with no present time don't count; ACCESS_LOST re-duplicates once; waits up to FRESH_WAIT_S (20 ms) for a frame shown at or after `after`, else the held frame is the screen as it is.
Copies the new frame into the duplication's own texture on the GPU and releases DXGI's at once; returns its present time (converted to time.monotonic).
DxgiShot.crops asks for boxes: each copied to a staging texture, optionally waited for on a fence (Dxgi._copied), mapped, and handed to convert as numpy views.
Any CaptureError closes the duplication and the shot is taken with mss for the next 10 s.

flows.title: A frame's re-finds in one C call
flows.summary: Every followed monster is re-found each frame in one native call on the C's own threads, optionally answered from the GPU, with Python's per-job work done as answers arrive.
flows.trigger: The frame step (localization.worldstate) asks the monster detector to re-find every track in a new frame.

steps.text: On first use makes native.Refinds(ready pictures, threads): native.lib() builds/loads native.c's DLL if needed; rf_open_as makes the context, the thread pool and, if gm_on, the GPU starter.
Takes the context's lock and calls rf_start with the frame, the RfJob array, the picture lists, THRESHOLD, REFIND_GOOD and NEAR_GOOD (and the token of a call sent ahead).
Validates the jobs, orders them largest first and wakes the pool; with the GPU on, gpumatch.c's gm_rf_send submits every window and picture in one submission.
For each job: the near window first (memo, else first pictures then next ones by the contract), the full window if the near answer isn't good enough.
With the GPU: a window's candidates within 2 GM_EPS of its best approximate score are scored exactly on the CPU; anything else is matched by the CPU (rf_best).
Hands each finished job's index back; Python checks the kind and starts fallbacks meanwhile, and the caller's thread matches a job itself when none is in.
Called once the caller is done: every job finished, memos of ids not in the call dropped (unless keep), the lock released by Refinds.end.

flows.title: Who plays: from --character to her files
flows.summary: A process resolves its character once, before physics loads, and every layer then reads the same profile.

steps.text: --character sets GAMELAB_CHARACTER (inherited by children) before motion.physics loads; refuses if physics already loaded as someone else.
GAMELAB_CHARACTER, else (unless GAMELAB_FIXED_STATS) lab/character.json, else config.toml [characters] default, else the thief.
Picks her class module, builds profile(id), applies stats (the thief's [character] and Lucky Seven level; others' tables over fixed stats) and configured(c, table).
For the magician: skill levels, Magic Claw's level and MP, buffs and Magic Guard's share, pet, keys and bottom-bar lines from [characters.magician].
Caches the Character for the process: motion.physics takes CHARACTER = active().stats; localization's trackers take its Shape.
Her own files: Files(perception.files): the thief's lab/ names, another's under lab/characters/<id>/.

not_done: The re-finds' GPU backend is off by default (lab/GPU or GAMELAB_GPU switch it on): at the RTX 3080's idle clocks it answers later than the C, and the cores it frees made nothing measurably smoother (README, The re-finds' matches on the GPU; The re-finds' GPU, twice as fast).
Matching on the captured texture itself (zero-copy from DXGI to the GPU backend) is left undone: exact, but for live only (README, The re-finds' GPU, twice as fast).
capture's `[capture] fence` (waiting for the copy on an ID3D11Fence) is off by default and not tried live yet.
window.SWITCH_FALLBACK (SwitchToThisWindow) is on but untried in game.
The magician's lock, delays, damage, miss, wand, pet and priors are placeholders until live measurements (classes/magician.py PLACEHOLDERS).
The perception service doesn't learn who plays from her bottom bar yet: in-game commands play another character only when GAMELAB_CHARACTER names her (character.py; README, Characters).
The exact finder has not been measured live or on any map but Tree Dungeon.
